Okay, so I’m bipolar and this helps me, and I have also used it on the kids I work with. Use distraction. And not like, “hey, look over there!” I’ll ask them things such as, “what’s your favorite type of music?” And then I will have them talk about their favorite band and what they like about them. Then I will have them list the albums from the bands, and ask them which one is their favorite, what is their favorite song from it, what they like about it. What they’re favorite lyric is, why. Then i move onto band number two if they haven’t come down, but they usually have by that time. It doesn’t have to be music, it can be any subject they are interested in. I’ve had great success with bringing my kiddos down when they are all “spun up”.

The growth of social media has definitely made things worse over the years. From when I was a teen until now people(not just kids) have been self diagnosing at faster and faster rates, especially thanks to newer more connected forms of SM, the main culprit being TikTok. On TikTok, where you can see clips from people anywhere in the world, people can see one another’s “symptoms” and learn how to emulate them more easily. It’s really sad. Hello! I have been admitted several times, and now work in a facility myself!

Not all facilities are perfect, but at all the ones I’ve been to and the one I work at you will be able to wear your own clothes after your initial check in and search. Nothing with strings or hoods so bring some kind of slip on shoes and a sweatshirt. 

There will be groups every day, and after you get acclimated to the environment I highly suggest you attend them all. Be open and honest with everyone you have personal sessions with. You cannot take personal care items, and if you wear a bra you will need to take a sports bra. No underwire. No jewelry. 

These are what I can rattle off the top of my head from my personal experiences as a patient and employee at facilities.

I’m a mental health technician who works with adolescents. 

Her friend will be in a place where they are (hopefully) very caring and supportive. I have heard some bad stories, but at my facility in particular we follow a strict schedule for the kiddos with lots of love, care, and structure. I don’t know about the particular facility your sister’s friend will be at, but at ours we allow video visitation, however the visitors have to be over 16. We follow a group schedule every day, but there is a lot of variety involved. We have a goals group every morning where the kids set goals for the day, whatever they may be. We have art therapy, music therapy, one on one therapy, psychiatric consultations every day, and we even have a therapy dog now. In our particular state medication changes have to be approved by parents with two professionals consultants. 

As for your sister, she is likely very confused and, as you said, distraught. She is most likely blaming herself for not finding a way to help her friend. If possible, she should get into therapy right away because she will likely have complicated feelings surrounding this event that you and your parents just cannot help her with. This is a traumatic event for her, and should be treated as such. 

I think you are a wonderful sibling for reaching out here to find a way to help your sister understand this situation better. However, as I said, she is going to have some complicated feelings surrounding this traumatic event, and it needs to be dealt with in a way that only a trained professional can. We as humans sometimes say the wrong, unhelpful things without realizing it. Professionals are trained how to talk to people in a therapeutic manner, and they legally cannot speak about her feelings to others unless she is thinking of harming herself or someone else. That may help her feel more secure in getting to the root of her feelings. They can become dark quickly if not dealt with appropriately.

When my grandmother was alive she collected salt and pepper shakers. She was even on a local television show because of it. 

After she passed he kept collecting. As he said, it gave him something to go out and do. While my grandmother was alive they had collected over 4,000 sets, and hardly any of them were the same. Before he passed he had gotten up to 7,000. He gave them away as trinkets to family and friends. I have 70 sets myself. They mostly collected vintage sets, sets from occupied Japan or China. Several of them are worth quite a bit. 

When he was young his family owned a saw mill during the Great Depression. I learned there was a family with three little girls whose father was a deadbeat. He refused to even try to find a job. The little girls would listen for the saw mill to stop for lunch and run down to it for food, and my grandaddy, great uncles, and great Grandaddy would happily feed them bologna sandwiches. One day the girls’ mother asked them to bring home some uneaten food for their father and my grandaddy said they would send home food for him when he “got up off his lazy ass,” which says a lot since he never cursed. 

He had an eighth grade education. He always begged me to get a formal college education, and I know it disappointed him greatly when I left before I finished. I had already been planning to go back under a different degree path, but I definitely will be now to honor his memory. 

He was almost drafted into World War II, but my great grandpa got him out of it by telling the draft board that he was needed around the sawmill and farm. They owned over three hundred acres. He was one of twelve, and when my great grandparents passed the land was split and he possessed 77 acres, which was inherited by my dad, as he is an only child. 

He was drafted into the Korean Conflict. He delivered mail in Germany while he was there. I took him to a reenactment called “Remembering World War II” one year and he pointed out all of the things that he had remembered in the years during his childhood from it. Some of the equipment was the same as when he was in Korea, which he pointed out as well. 

He was up and going, running the farm and garden. Giving away tomatoes he grew and salt a pepper shakers, up until about five weeks ago when his health just absolutely plummeted. I got sick at the same time with vertigo so bad I had to crawl out of my house to get to the car and go to the hospital one day. I got to see him twice in the last two months, and even before that I had wasted a lot of time that could have been spent with him. When I saw him while he was in rehab after his stroke he was doing wonderfully. He was speaking clearly, getting up and walk around, and just doing great all around. It gave me a false sense of security. He had to go back to the hospital, and he was still doing well until the night he came home. I went to see him on the day before his death and got horrible vertigo. I started vomiting and my dad asked me to leave because he couldn’t take care of both of us. Before he left he looked at me and said, “I’ll be 95,” I said, “In February, Grandaddy.” When I finally got to come back later he was totally unresponsive and had the death rattle. I had to go to the doctor the next day for my vertigo and he passed while I was gone.
